findings.source_passage: "Didn't I tell you so?" said Flask; "yes, you'll soon see this right whale's head hoisted up opposite that parmacetti's."
findings.source_locator: Near end, after boats hailed to tow
findings.why_it_matters: The line 'hoisted up opposite that parmacetti's' is characteristic Flask dialect and directly sets up the Locke/Kant allegory; the draft drops it, weakening the transition.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Flask's exact words including 'opposite that parmacetti's' before the Locke/Kant passage.

findings.source_passage: "Do I suppose it? You'll know it before long, Flask...take it to the capstan, and give him such a wrenching and heaving, that his tail will come short off at the stump—do you see; and then, I rather guess when he finds himself docked in that queer fashion, he'll sneak off without the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs."
findings.source_locator: Long Stubb speech near end of dialogue
findings.why_it_matters: The comic grotesque detail—'sneak off without the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs'—is signature Melville burlesque; the draft truncates the speech and loses this punchline entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the tail-between-legs punchline and the ensuing rapid-fire exchange about selling the tail for an ox whip.

findings.source_passage: "And what will you do with the tail, Stubb?" "Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home;—what else?" "Now, do you mean what you say..." "Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship."
findings.source_locator: Final exchanges of the Stubb-Flask dialogue
findings.why_it_matters: This rapid-fire coda—ox-whip punchline and the dismissive 'Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship'—is a rhetorical cap on the comic theology; its absence flattens the scene's ending.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the ox-whip exchange and Stubb's closing 'Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship' before the boats are hailed.

findings.source_passage: Did you ever notice how that tusk of his is a sort of carved into a snake's head, Stubb?
findings.why_it_matters: The snake's-head tusk detail is a specific Fedallah characterization motif; its loss slightly thins the devilry imagery that the scene is building.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert a brief mention of the snake's-head tusk in Flask's description of Fedallah.

summary: The draft is largely faithful and preserves the key signatures (Locke/Kant, Fedallah shadow, core devil-swap dialogue), but suffers medium-level flattening in the comic tail-disposal exchanges and Flask's parmacetti line, with the ox-whip coda and the 'tail between his legs' punchline absent entirely.
